review.reviewBody: I used to spend hours every week ordering food. Now it's simple, super easy, and I have free time to spend on other aspects of my restaurant.

@graph.name: Agreeing the path takes one conversation
@graph.description: There is nothing to diagram and no process to write up. You tell us two things, we do the rest.

step.name: What each account can order
step.text: A guide per customer: items, your prices, your codes. However it is held today usually works.

step.name: Where finished orders land
step.text: The same destination for every account: an inbox, QuickBooks, EDI or the API. That decision is the whole workflow design.

step.name: We set each account up and off it goes
step.text: For most distributors the whole thing takes 24 to 48 hours. Buyers get the app and usually order the same day.

@graph.name: Is VOS distribution workflow software in the usual sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not in the sense of a tool you design processes in. There is no canvas, no rules engine, no task queue and no approval chain here. What VOS does is make one leg of the path fixed: how a customer's order is created and how it reaches you. Everything downstream stays yours to run.

@graph.name: Can we build different paths for different accounts?

acceptedAnswer.text: The guide is per account, so what a customer can order and at what price varies. Where a completed order goes is agreed with us up front, so it lands the same way whoever is on shift. Fewer variations is the point, and it is why this needs no maintenance.

@graph.name: Who handles it when an item is out?

acceptedAnswer.text: A person on your team, as now. VOS does not decide substitutions or notify anybody on your behalf. The difference is that orders tend to arrive earlier and stock levels are visible beside them, so the decision happens before picking rather than during it.

@graph.name: Do we need to write the process down first?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, and that is much of the appeal. Adopting distribution workflow software normally starts with weeks of mapping. Here you decide two things, the guides and the delivery method, and the path follows from those.

@graph.name: How does this work while half our accounts still phone?

acceptedAnswer.text: You will be running two paths for a while, and it is better to admit that than pretend otherwise. Calls get written up as they are now, with no reference or send time attached. The app path grows as accounts move across.

@graph.name: Does it connect to the systems we already use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, by whichever single route suits you: by email as a PDF, Excel or Word file, through EDI, into QuickBooks, or straight into your ERP over the API. Take one of the direct feeds and there is no entry step at all.

@graph.name: Will our staff have to work differently?

acceptedAnswer.text: They work in the same systems they do now. What changes is what turns up in them: finished, coded orders in place of messages to interpret. Nobody has to learn a new screen on your side of the path.

@graph.name: What size of distributor is this aimed at?

acceptedAnswer.text: Smaller food distributors, independents and DSD rounds included. You need no IT staff, nobody to own the process and no enterprise contract, and we quote per distributor rather than publishing a price list.
